title: I should never have clicked send

fn.en: Talk about behaviour on social media; criticize past actions.

gr: should have and shouldn’t have for looking back at a past action

can.en: I can look back at something I did and say what I should have done instead.

acts.say: Say honestly whether you have ever done any of the left-hand ones.

items.x: Posting a video of a party your boss can see.
Sharing a photograph of a cat.
Tweeting about a rude interviewer the same evening.
Telling your boss you are ill and then posting from a match.
Asking a question in a work group chat.

using messages online to frighten or hurt somebody

sub.en: It has already happened. You are saying what would have been better.

items.q: She ___ more careful when she posted the video.
items.why: should have + past participle looks back at a past action and criticizes it.

items.q: She ___ her boss as a friend online in the first place.
You ___ asked for an extension earlier — it was still possible then.
items.why: could have + past participle = it was possible and you did not do it. Never write could of.

items.q: I ___ clicked send. That is the only thing I would change.
That ___ of me. I am sorry.

items.why: If only + past perfect expresses regret about the past, like the third conditional.

items.q: If he ___ waited a day, he ___ the job.

items.why: The action is finished, so should have + past participle is needed.
could of is never correct — it only sounds like could have.

w: he would have got the job
items.why: RECYCLED from Lesson 31: the if clause never takes would have.

tts: I accidentally posted a video of myself and some friends at a party, and my boss saw it. I didn’t mean to post it — I was uploading a different video and clicked on this one too. It was really embarrassing, and now my boss thinks I’m unprofessional.
I had just had a job interview, and one of the interviewers was very rude to me. So I tweeted about it. As soon as I pressed send, I knew it was a mistake, but it was too late.
Later I found out that I would have been offered the job, but somebody saw my tweet and they changed their minds and gave it to somebody else.

items.q: How did the first speaker post the video?
o: By accident, while uploading a different one

items.q: When did the second speaker realize his mistake?
o: As soon as he pressed send

items.q: What was the consequence for the second speaker?
o: He lost a job he would otherwise have been offered

tts: I really wanted to go to a big football game, but I was supposed to be working. So I told my boss I was ill.
The game was brilliant, but unfortunately I got so excited I started tweeting about it, and my boss saw the tweets, so she knew I wasn’t at home sick. I ended up losing my job.
It really wasn’t my fault. I was looking after my parents’ house while they were away, and I decided to have a party.
It was only going to be a few friends, but one of my friends wrote about it online. He didn’t realize it, but that meant five hundred people knew, and about a hundred and fifty turned up.

The boss found out because of the tweets.

write.q: Write about something you sent, posted or said that you would take back. Use should have and shouldn’t have at least twice each, one could have, and one third conditional showing what would have followed.
plan: what you should have done instead
what was possible and you did not do
write.model: A few years ago I replied to a work email at eleven at night, and I replied to everybody rather than to one person. The message itself was not rude, but it made it very clear that I disagreed with my manager in front of nine other people. I should have read the addresses before I pressed send, and I should never have written anything at that hour in the first place. That was careless of me. I could have saved it as a draft and looked at it in the morning, which is what I do now with anything that matters. If I had waited eight hours, I would have deleted three of the sentences and probably sent nothing at all. If only I had gone to bed.

speak.q: Tell the story out loud in about a minute. Say what you did, what you should have done, and what would have happened if you had.
speak.model: A few years ago I replied to a work email at eleven at night — and hit reply-all. It wasn’t rude, but it made it obvious I disagreed with my manager, in front of nine people. I should have read the addresses. I should never have written anything at that hour. I could have saved it as a draft. If I’d waited eight hours, I’d have deleted half of it and probably sent nothing.
